name: Pearling

card.summary: A body modification in which small beads are placed permanently under the skin of the genitals, done partly for appearance.
card.note: Implant procedure with inflammation common during healing and occasional rejection.

quick.overview:
Pearling, also called genital beading, is a body modification in which small beads of materials such as Teflon, silicone, surgical steel or titanium are inserted under the skin of the genitals. It is done partly for the changed look of the area and is usually intended to alter a partner's sensation.

It has a long cultural history, with Chinese records from the early 1400s describing it as imported from Southeast Asia. No clinical studies of outcomes are known.
quick.how: Two broad procedure types exist, one resembling a frenum piercing and one resembling a subdermal implant, the latter needing more medical knowledge and specialised tools. Beads are chosen from implant-type materials; this entry gives no procedural instructions.
quick.risks: Commentary describes risks and healing similar to subdermal implants elsewhere on the body. Inflammation is very common during and after healing, and rejection is rare but can occur.

lead: Pearling (genital beading) is a body modification in which small beads are permanently inserted under the skin of the genitals. It is practised partly for appearance and usually with a partner's sensation in mind [1].

Implant materials include Teflon, silicone, surgical steel and titanium; early versions used pearls, which gave the practice its name [1]. The origin is unknown. Chinese documents from the early 1400s describe it as imported from Southeast Asia, and Antonio Pigafetta, chronicler of Magellan's voyage, recorded it [1].
No clinical studies of the practice are known.

angle.text: The implants permanently change the contour of the area, which is the appearance goal alongside the sensory one.

paras: The Chinese term for the inserts translates roughly as Burmese bells [1]. The historian William Henry Scott wrote of pins inserted in young boys in the Visayas, later replaced by decorated rings [1].
Yakuza members are reported to practise it in prison, with each bead said to represent a year served, and a 2013 Atlantic article reported Filipino sailors using it to stand out [1].

Wikipedia describes either procedure as relatively safe, with healing similar to subdermal implants and shortened by genital blood flow. Inflammation is very common during healing, aftercare can reduce it, and rejection is rare but possible. The article cites no clinical outcome data [1].

timeline.event: Chinese documents describe the practice as imported from Southeast Asia [1]
